The title is dismissed by the two voices who take it up. Keil and Delitzsch call the Greek inscription assigning the psalm to David through Jeremiah erroneous, since Jeremiah never was a Babylonian exile, and find the date in the language instead, a thrice-repeated particle and a lengthened verb form fitting the period the contents require. Adam Clarke is blunter, calling the ascription ridiculous and observing that anachronism in the psalm titles was of no importance to whoever wrote them; the Hebrew and Chaldee have no title and the Syriac gives David, and whether it was sung during the captivity or after he thinks of little consequence.

Why the exiles were beside the water is variously answered. Matthew Henry takes the harder view, that they were quartered there to be worked in the galleys, or placed there as the most melancholy spot: houses, if built, were not to stand in the cities, the places of concourse, but by the rivers, the places of solitude, where the exiles might mingle their tears with the streams. C.H. Spurgeon has them glad to be out of the noisy streets, sitting in little groups to make common lamentation where the water's flow seemed in sympathy with their weeping. John Calvin offers a liturgical reason: synagogues were commonly built near rivers for Jews who had to wash before prayer, and having none in Babylon they resorted to such sites and served God in the open air; an early Greek father conjectured that they were at first not suffered to live in their conquerors' cities but dispersed along the rivers. John Wesley says only that sitting was the mourner's usual posture; Charles Ellicott names the rivers as the country's characteristic feature, much as one speaks of the mountains of Wales.

Augustine reads the scene as allegory. The waters of Babylon, he says, are all the things loved here that pass away: one man loves husbandry and grows rich by it, another thinks it grand to be a soldier, and each loves a stream of Babylon, not a foundation of Jerusalem. The citizens of the holy city who understand their captivity watch how men's lusts drag them about and drive them into the sea, and do not throw themselves in but sit down and weep — for those carried away, or for themselves, whose deserts have placed them there.

Two details are disputed. On the tree, John Gill and Clarke keep the willow, Clarke reporting that willows grew in such quantity on the Euphrates that a prophet called it the river of willows; Ellicott denies it, since the willow is not found in Babylonia and the tree must be the poplar, and suggests identifying it may not matter, the picture being a poetical way of saying that all religious and festal song fell silent. Clarke reconstructs the moment: resting after their toil and meaning to spend the time religiously, they took the harps and were about to sing, then thought of their own country and were so filled with distress that they unstrung them with one consent and hung them up.

The demand for a song draws the sharpest writing here. Ellicott corrects the second verb, which the ancient versions treated as a synonym of the first: better is they that make us howl, so the men whose oppression had drawn the wild eastern scream of lamentation were now asking for mirth. Clarke calls the demand as unreasonable as it was insulting, and turns the reply into a set piece, hearing a deep sigh in the guttural sound of the opening word and repeating the pronoun through a list — we in slavery, exiled, stripped of property, deprived of our worship, insulted, among heathens — before concluding that God does not expect it, man should not wish it, and it is base in an enemy to require it.
5:
The oath about forgetting Jerusalem is read by Adam Clarke as a refusal of accommodation: to sing on demand would renounce the land and acknowledge that the singers had made peace with bondage. He turns the two curses into a catalogue of losses — let me forget my right hand and lose my skill with the harp if ever I prostitute it to please the ungodly, and lose my voice, my tongue and its faculty of speech, my ear and its discernment of sounds — and calls the sentiment truly patriotic and dignified, such words being found only in the mouths of slaves whom the grace of God has made free. Charles Ellicott keeps the figure narrower, taking the cunning for skill on the harp: if the poet could so far forget Jerusalem's bondage as to strike the strings in joy, let his hand lose for ever the skill to touch them. John Wesley reduces it to a valuation, that Jerusalem's prosperity is worth more than all other delights.

On Edom the voices are historical before moral. Ellicott points to one prophet as the best comment, quoting the charge that Edom stood on the other side while strangers carried away Jacob's forces, and adds that the word for rasing means to make bare. C.H. Spurgeon supplies the family history: the Edomites owed friendship by kinship, but the elder never loved to serve the younger, so when Jacob's day of trouble came Esau profited by it. Matthew Henry adds what the cry accomplished: it made the Chaldean army more furious when it was already so enraged it needed no spur.

The closing beatitude is where the commentators part company: is it revenge? Henry insists it is not: the exiles please themselves with the prospect of their enemies' ruin from a holy zeal for God's glory and not from any spirit of revenge, and states the rule plainly: vengeance belongs to God, and we may not pray for the ruin of the church's enemies even while praying for her success. Gill takes the same line and defends the justice: a just retaliation, since the Babylonians had done this to Jewish children, and what is desired is the glory of divine justice rather than private satisfaction. Clarke removes the difficulty by changing the sentence's mood, holding these to be prophetic declarations of what retributive providence would bring about, with no incitement to cruelty, so that praying for the destruction of one's enemies is, as he puts it, totally out of the question. Ellicott alone declines the defence and names the thing: the luxury of revenge is well expressed in this beatitude, pronounced on the man who can carry the law of retaliation to its bitter end, and commentators have in turn tried to disguise and to justify the passion.

The description of Babylon is textually uncertain, and Ellicott sets out the range: our version follows one Greek translator, two others give wasted, another robber, the Greek and Latin wretched. As pointed the word must be a passive participle, though he is careful that a Hebrew would speak so of a doom foreseen but not yet accomplished, and quotes an Arabic saying about pursuing the man already as good as caught. Clarke identifies the man called happy as Cyrus, God's chosen agent, and traces the city's decline from that capture until nothing remained. Keil and Delitzsch print the last two verses without comment, the block breaking off at the quotation. At the last clause Ellicott glosses the children as sucklings, prefers cliff to stones, calls the practice a feature of the cruelty with which ancient war was cursed, and finds the same horror in a line of Homer. Gill reports an allegorical reading taking the little ones for the first motions of sin, to be crushed at their rising, and declines it: such a sense seems to have no place here.
